To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the proteasome is involved in the pathogenic process of prion diseases and, conversely, that prion proteins interact and affect the proteasome functionality.

(i) Prion proteins coprecipitate and colocalize with the 20s proteasome, (ii) the proteasome activity is enhanced during scrapie disease, (iii) Prion proteins interact with the 20 proteasomes and induce a decrease in proteasome functionality.

the proteasome‐prion interaction is a two‐way process: on the one hand, PrPSc increases the proteasome activity, and, on the other hand, the proteasome degrades PrPSc, which is also the key factor for the disease progression.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the proteasome during scrapie disease.
the relationship between the 20S complex and the pathological isoform of PrP, which may be of interest for the development of new therapies for neurodegenerative diseases.
the role of 20S proteases in prion disease and their possible use as therapeutic agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
prion‐induced proteasome activation leads to a compensatory mechanism that, in turn, induces apoptosis.
prions are not only substrates for the 20S complex, but they are also able to interact with the proteasomal complex and affect its functionality.
the proteasome‐prion interaction is a complex process that can be modulated by the cellular environment and by the proteasomal composition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
proteasome activity increases in scrapie disease, and that this increase is associated with an interaction between the 20S and prions.
prions and the proteasome interact, affecting proteasome functionality and, thus, neuronal homeostasis.
the proteasome is a target of PrPC and PrPSc.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proteasome is a key player in the pathogenesis of scrapie.
the 20S and 26S proteasomes are involved in prion diseases and that the proteasome‐prion interaction is a two‐way street.
the 20S complex is not a mere scaffold for the 19S complex, but that it has its own activity, which is regulated by the 19S.
